extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars of political theory and constitution-makers (practical statesmen of city-states)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on structuring magistracies, courts, methods of appointment, and the causes and remedies of revolutions in states; oriented to evaluating how institutional arrangements suit different regimes. Useful for analysing or designing constitutions for cities/polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of deliberative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide in whose hands the deliberative power of the state shall be (people at large, magistrates, or mixed arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People may be allowed to have a vote on proposed bills but not the power to originate proposals; they may give advice while determining power remains with magistrates. In oligarchies allow the people a place in administration without enabling disorder by calling some commoners to council, establishing pre-advisers/guardians to propose first what shall be enacted, or by letting the people vote on propositions but not propose contrary measures. In democracies follow opposite practices (e.g., powers of pardoning vs. condemning differ between forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of pardon and condemnation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Which body has the power to pardon or condemn differs by regime and must be allocated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In oligarchies the people should be allowed the power of pardoning but not of condemning (causes referred back to magistrates); in republics (democracies) pardoning is with the few but condemning is referred to the people at large. Allocate these judicial/political prerogatives to avoid unstable concentrations of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of magistracy (who counts as a magistrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates are most properly those who sit on the deliberative council, decide causes, or are in command (command being especially peculiar to magistrates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish civil magistrates from priests, choregi, heralds, ambassadors, economic officers (e.g., corn-meters), servile offices, and military commanders where multiple citizens obey one general. Practical institutional design should focus on offices whose function is deliberation, adjudication, or command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of offices and term length
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many magistrates there should be, what each office's functions are, and how long each magistrate should hold office (ranges: six months, shorter, a year, long, perpetual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide also whether the same person may hold the same office multiple times or only once. The design must consider community size: extensive governments should allot one employment to one person; small states may require a few citizens to execute many employments to avoid shortage of eligible officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization vs. multiplicity of roles
rubrics_metrics.description: In large polities, assign single employments to individuals; in small polities, allow individuals to hold multiple offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything tends to be better done when a single person can give whole attention to one employment; but where numbers are small it is necessary and not inconvenient to intrust different charges to the same person if they do not interfere with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional clarity for tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which tribunals should adjudicate which matters and whether jurisdiction should be uniform or specialized by fact or parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the same magistrate should hear a cause wherever it arises (e.g., decency of manners in market vs elsewhere), or whether distinctions should be made based on the fact, the parties (man vs woman), or the place. Properly delineate jurisdiction to avoid conflicts and ensure consistent adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of magistrates to regime character
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates to be appointed should reflect the nature of the government: aristocracy -> well-educated, oligarchy -> rich, democracy -> freemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices are peculiar to certain states (e.g., pre-advisers in oligarchies; a senate in democracies). Choose kinds of magistracies and their personnel so they correspond to the community's composition and nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-fold classification of magistrate differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates differ in (1) who appoints them, (2) who is eligible/appointed, and (3) the mode of appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these three axes can vary: appointing body may be all citizens, some out of whole body, or some from a particular order (by fortune, family, virtue, etc.); mode may be by vote or lot. Combinations of these produce diverse institutional variants; choose consistently according to regime aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of appointment (vote vs lot and combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates may be chosen by vote or lot, by all citizens or parts thereof; different blends and subdivisions (tribes/wards/companies) create multiple legitimate methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are up to twelve methods when mixing who elects (all, part, particular ranks) with vote/lot choices. Democracies suit methods where all elect magistrates out of the whole people either by vote or lot (or some by one method and some by the other). Oligarchies tend to favor selection out of certain ranks and lot is often most correspondent to oligarchy; aristocracies favor the whole community electing magistrates out of particular persons by vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magistracy power allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign particular provinces (powers) to magistrates (e.g., finance management vs laws) according to office type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different magistracies should have clearly defined powers; for instance a general's power is different from a clerk of the market. Establish who has command, deliberation, or adjudication responsibility to avoid overlap and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization and number of courts
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-ordered judicial system should comprise eight courts addressing distinct classes of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eight are: (1) court inspecting magistrates after office; (2) court to punish those injuring the public; (3) court for causes where the state is a party; (4) court deciding between magistrates and private persons appealing fines; (5) court for disputes over large-value contracts; (6) court to judge murders (various species) and foreigners; (7) special court (e.g., Phreattae) for murders by fugitives to decide return; (8) small-claims court for actions of 1–5 drachmas (or slightly more). Decide whether these may be tried by same or different judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and composition of judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who the judges shall be (whole people or particulars), how many courts are necessary, and whether judges are chosen by vote or lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are four sorts of judges depending on whether selection is by all or part, and by vote or lot. Different causes may be allocated to different selecting methods (some causes judged by whole community, others by specific persons), and different regimes favour different arrangements: all-judges-in-all-causes suits democracy; certain persons judging all causes suits oligarchy; mixed arrangements suit aristocracy or free states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid founding a government on incorrect equality assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume equality in one respect (e.g., liberty) implies equality in all respects; misapplied equality causes instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracies arise when people wrongly extend equality in liberty to equality in everything; oligarchies arise when inequality in fortune is assumed to imply inequality in all respects. Establish which matters require equality in number versus equality in value (proportion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize principal causes of sedition and revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedition most commonly arises from desires about equality or superiority; principal proximate causes include profit, honour, haughtiness, fear, eminence, contempt, and disproportionate growth of some part of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider election intrigues, neglect, shortage of numbers, and excessive dissimilarity of circumstances. Examples: demagogues provoking confiscations; nobles conspiring when insulted; disproportionate increase of the poor in democracies leading to instability. Diagnose these causes to target remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish equality in number vs equality in value
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality may be of number (same parts/quantity) or of value (proportional equality); different political questions require different kinds of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply proportionate allocation (e.g., representation, honors) where value demands it rather than numeric equality everywhere. Failure to apply the correct kind of equality fuels disputes over proportionate shares in administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative stability of regime types
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies are generally safer and less liable to sedition than oligarchies; governments of moderate fortunes are safest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchies are vulnerable to internal conspiracies among the few or conspiracies of the few against the people; democracies are mainly at risk from the few aiming for exclusive power. Favor institutions that avoid extreme concentrations of wealth or privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-treatment, profit-seeking and honours as triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates' avarice, unjust honours or exclusions, and ill-treatment are common triggers for sedition and revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avaricious magistrates who enrich themselves privately or at public expense provoke sedition against the state or among magistrates. Excessive honours that make individuals greater than the state can lead to tyranny; ostracism and preventative design choices may be better than corrective measures after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor disputes among elites must be checked early
rubrics_metrics.description: Quarrels among leading citizens often expand into full revolutions; suppress or reconcile early disputes among the powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small beginnings are half the business — smother quarrels early to prevent city-wide factionalism. Examples include revolutions begun from love affairs, inheritance quarrels, or matrimonial disputes which drew city factions in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues and mechanisms of democratic overthrow
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies, demagogues can cause revolutions by informing against wealthy citizens, distributing bribes, or using confiscations to drive elites into conspiracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demagogues may create tyranny when they combine military power with popular influence; modern rhetorical demagogues less able to seize military power but still potent politically. Anticipate tactics like bribery to avoid trierarch payments, false promises of foreign support, or confiscatory laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of regime change: violence and fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions occur either by violence or by fraud; fraud itself can be (a) deceiving the people into consenting, then forcing compliance, or (b) persuading the people then coercing permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: the Four Hundred deceived the people with false promises of Persian support, then tried to keep power. Anticipate and guard against both violent coups and fraudulent manipulations of public consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-political/accidental causes of regime change
rubrics_metrics.description: Population losses, migrations, or accidental demographic shifts (battle casualties, colonization choices) can alter the balance of factions and thereby the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include heavy battlefield losses of elites transforming an oligarchy into a democracy; admitting new citizen groups or strangers may introduce factional tensions leading to expulsions or revolutions. Institutional design should account for resilience to demographic shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow institutional erosion by neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, neglected procedural changes (e.g., changing elections from votes to lots) or gradual decay of censuses/civic qualifications can silently alter a constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard the small procedural rules that preserve balance; reforms that seem minor can enable new factions to seize office. Example: elections changed to lot allowed meaner people to gain office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who make the state powerful tend to claim rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person or group who has recently been the cause of the state's power or success will seek dominant place in its government and may provoke disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victors in war, prominent tribes, magistrates who increased the state's prestige, or groups who provided key public services are likely to agitate for political advantage; anticipate and structure institutions to channel reward without destabilizing the constitution.
